findings.title: Dayjs objects compared with === always returns false
findings.body: The expression `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` uses strict equality (`===`) to compare two Dayjs instances. Since these are distinct object references, this comparison always evaluates to `false`, regardless of whether the two moments represent the same point in time. The intended check (whether start equals end, indicating an "unavailable" date override) will never trigger. Use `.isSame()` instead.

findings.title: Copy-paste error: `end` computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
findings.body: In the working hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` uses `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`. This means the end of the slot is never actually checked against working hour boundaries—only the start time is checked twice. A slot that starts within working hours but extends past the end of the working window would incorrectly pass this check.

findings.title: Working hours check logic is inverted: marks slot unavailable if outside ANY single working hour entry
findings.body: The code uses `workingHours.find(...)` to return `true` if the slot is outside a particular working hour entry, then treats a match as "slot is outside working hours → return false (unavailable)." When a user has multiple working hour entries for the same day (e.g., 9–12 and 14–18), a slot at 10:00 is outside the 14–18 entry, so `find` returns that entry and the slot is incorrectly marked unavailable. The correct logic should check that the slot is not inside ANY working hour entry (i.e., use `!workingHours.some(...)` with an "is inside" predicate).

findings.title: Potential runtime error when override.timeZone is undefined
findings.body: `override.timeZone` is typed as optional (`timeZone?: string` in `TimeRange`). If a `DateOverride` object does not have `timeZone` set (which is possible since the field was just added and is optional), `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(undefined)` will be called. Depending on the dayjs timezone plugin version, this may throw an exception or produce an incorrect offset, causing slot generation to fail silently or crash.

findings.title: dateOverrides.find() uses side-effect mutation of dateOverrideExist but find short-circuits unpredictably
findings.body: The variable `dateOverrideExist` is set to `true` inside the `find` callback as a side effect. However, `find` stops iterating as soon as the callback returns a truthy value. If the first date override matches the day but the slot IS within it (callback returns undefined/falsy), `dateOverrideExist` is set to true and iteration continues. But if a second override for a different day is encountered, the day check fails and `dateOverrideExist` remains true from the first override. If no override returns `true` from `find`, the code falls through to `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;`—which is correct. However, if the first override matches the day and the slot is within it, but a later override for the SAME day has the slot outside it, `find` returns that later override and the function returns `false`. This is correct for a single user, but the interplay between the side-effect flag and `find`'s short-circuit behavior makes the logic fragile and hard to reason about, and could produce wrong results if overrides are not sorted by relevance.
